strengths: The behavioral reconstruction objective is a sensible alternative to reconstructing policy weights: it permits different parameterizations to reproduce similar actions and provides a compact search space for downstream optimization.

The experiments demonstrate useful low-dimensional policy representations and rapid initial learning on several Mountain Car and modified Reacher tasks. The failure on Mountain Car height is acknowledged explicitly.

The Mountain Car study varies policy size, dataset size, and latent dimension. Multiple seeds, confidence intervals, additional baseline results, and substantial implementation details improve the empirical presentation.
weaknesses: The central expressivity claim is not established by the evaluation. Appendix B defines performance recovery as (ubL − lbD)/(ubD − lbD), which measures the best decoded return relative to the dataset's return range. A representation retaining only a few high-return behaviors could score well while losing most policies. Held-out behavioral reconstruction, occupancy coverage, and preservation across a broader reward family are needed to support compression of the policy space.

The connection between the practical loss and the formal objective is insufficiently justified. Section 4 replaces occupancy divergence with action-space distance on sampled states, but the cited divergence bound does not establish a bound for this empirical squared-error surrogate with deterministic policies. In Reacher, uniform sampling of the six-dimensional bounding box also produces invalid sine/cosine combinations, so reconstruction quality on these inputs need not reflect behavior on reachable states.

The intrinsic-dimension conclusion substantially exceeds the evidence. Only two simple environments are studied, and network-size variation is examined only in Mountain Car. Compressing a filtered collection of randomly sampled networks does not establish the dimension of all realizable behaviors or its independence from network size. Neither quantitative intrinsic-dimension estimates nor reconstruction-versus-dimension curves are provided.

Essential comparisons and ablations are missing. There is no matched parameter-reconstruction autoencoder, removal of novelty filtering, random low-dimensional subspace, or direct comparison with prior policy-manifold methods. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate the contribution of the behavioral loss or establish an advantage over the closely related approaches discussed in Appendix A.

The downstream comparisons primarily pit the pretrained representation against algorithms learning from scratch. Comparisons with reward-free skill learning, search over the collected policy archive, and simple latent-space search would clarify whether the gains arise from the proposed representation or from access to a useful policy collection. Pretraining costs are not separated sufficiently to assess end-to-end computational efficiency or amortization across tasks.

The headline 121801:1 compression ratio describes the number of policy parameters per latent coordinate, not total model storage or demonstrated preservation of functional expressivity. The large shared decoder remains necessary, and several Table 1 configurations have poor recovery even under the permissive best-return metric. The abstract and conclusions should distinguish search-dimension reduction from comprehensive behavioral compression.

Several reporting inconsistencies impair reproducibility: the main text says Mountain Car speed and height do not terminate early, whereas Appendix B says they terminate at the right goal; Figure 4 reports 10 runs while the appendix describes 75 fine-tuning runs on 75 autoencoders without explaining the relationship; and the Reacher clockwise condition is written as tangential velocity greater than −11. These details need clarification.

strengths: The behavioral reconstruction objective is a sensible alternative to reconstructing policy weights: it allows different parameterizations to represent similar action functions.
The pipeline is straightforward and modular. Experiments vary policy size, dataset size, and latent dimension, and demonstrate that very low-dimensional codes can retain useful policies.

The downstream experiments show promising early learning on several tasks, include multiple established RL baselines, and report uncertainty across runs. The appendix provides substantial implementation details and acknowledges failures caused by insufficient dataset coverage.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation does not establish preservation of behavioral expressivity. Appendix B defines performance recovery as (best decoded return − worst dataset return)/(best dataset return − worst dataset return). This measures recovery of a task-specific maximum; a representation containing only a few successful policies could score highly while discarding most behaviors. Held-out reconstruction errors, occupancy-distribution comparisons, and behavioral coverage measurements are missing.

The central intrinsic-dimension claim exceeds the evidence. Experiments cover only Mountain Car and a modified Reacher, with policy-size variation confined to Mountain Car. Compressing a selected collection of randomly generated policies does not demonstrate that the full realizable behavior space has low dimension independent of network size. There is no direct intrinsic-dimension estimate or controlled study of environmental complexity.

The connection between the practical loss and the stated behavior-space objective is insufficiently justified. The cited policy-divergence bound does not establish an occupancy-divergence guarantee for finite-state action MSE. Moreover, maximizing an upper bound does not guarantee increased occupancy diversity. Reacher states are sampled uniformly from a bounding box over sine and cosine coordinates, so most sampled points violate the physical angle constraints; the relevance of reconstruction on these points is untested.

Essential comparisons and ablations are absent. There is no parameter-reconstruction autoencoder baseline, random low-dimensional subspace baseline, unfiltered-dataset ablation, or comparison with related latent-policy and unsupervised skill-learning methods. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate the benefit of the behavioral loss, novelty filtering, or learned representation over simpler alternatives.

The sample-efficiency evidence concerns downstream adaptation rather than the full pipeline. Comparisons omit a breakdown of dataset construction and autoencoder training costs and do not compare against methods receiving comparable pretraining resources. Final performance is also mixed: conventional baselines outperform latent PGPE on some tasks, including Mountain Car speed and height. The broad claims of superior efficiency and performance therefore need qualification.

The headline 121,801:1 compression ratio counts policy parameters versus latent coordinates, excluding the shared decoder and the full policy it generates. It demonstrates reduced search dimensionality, but does not establish equivalent storage or inference savings. Combined with the weak expressivity metric, the five-orders-of-magnitude claim is easy to overinterpret.

Several experimental details are inconsistent or ambiguous. The main text and appendix disagree about termination in Mountain Car speed and height; the clockwise reward condition is unclear; and Appendix B describes 75 Mountain Car runs while the main plots report 10, without explaining the selection or aggregation. These issues impede independent interpretation and reproduction.

strengths: The behavioral reconstruction objective is a sensible and potentially useful alternative to reconstructing policy weights: it allows different parameterizations to represent similar action mappings.

The pipeline combines reward-free policy collection, latent representation learning, and downstream optimization coherently. Applying PGPE in the learned latent space is straightforward and practically motivated.

The experiments show promising early learning performance on several tasks, with studies across policy sizes, dataset sizes, and latent dimensions. Confidence intervals, architectural details, and baseline hyperparameters are provided.

The paper explicitly acknowledges an important limitation: behaviors poorly represented in the policy dataset may remain inaccessible during downstream optimization, as illustrated by Mountain Car height.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving policy-space expressivity is not adequately evaluated. The performance-recovery metric compares the best decoded return against the dataset's return range on a few rewards; it does not measure reconstruction of individual policies, occupancy-distribution coverage, or preservation of behavioral diversity. High recovery can therefore coexist with losing most behaviors. Held-out behavioral reconstruction and coverage measurements are needed.

The evidence does not establish that intrinsic behavioral dimension depends mainly on environment complexity rather than network size. Experiments cover only Mountain Car and a modified two-joint Reacher, with the policy-size sweep restricted to Mountain Car. Compressing a sampled, novelty-filtered distribution of random policies does not establish the dimensionality of all realizable behaviors. No intrinsic-dimension estimate or controlled complexity study is provided.

The connection between the formal occupancy-divergence objective and the implemented action-MSE loss is insufficiently justified. The cited divergence bound does not by itself establish a bound for squared action differences between deterministic policies. Moreover, Reacher states are sampled independently from a bounding box, violating the sine/cosine constraints of valid observations. Accuracy on these artificial states need not imply fidelity on visited trajectories, and the reconstruction objective does not explicitly enforce that equivalent policies receive nearby latent codes.

Essential comparisons and ablations are missing. There is no direct comparison with parameter-reconstruction autoencoders, prior latent-policy methods, random low-dimensional parameterizations, or unsupervised skill-learning approaches. Ablating novelty filtering and the behavioral loss would help establish which components account for the results. The current comparisons against conventional RL algorithms do not isolate the proposed contribution.

The downstream results support a narrower claim than general superiority in sample efficiency. Faster early improvement sometimes comes with lower final returns, and height fails substantially. The evaluation reports downstream interaction counts without a clear breakdown of preprocessing and representation-training costs or their amortization across tasks. Broader continuous-control experiments and matched-pretraining comparisons are needed.

The advertised 121801:1 compression measures the ratio of policy parameters to latent coordinates, not total model storage or computation: the decoder still generates a full policy and must itself be retained. This is a useful reduction in optimization dimension, but the paper should distinguish it from model compression and qualify the claim that most expressivity is retained.

strengths: The behavioral reconstruction objective is a sensible alternative to reconstructing policy weights: it allows different parameterizations to represent similar functions and supports reward-free representation learning without expert policies.

The experiments demonstrate that very low-dimensional latent codes can generate useful policies. Latent PGPE shows promising early learning performance on several Mountain Car and Reacher tasks, with multiple seeds and confidence intervals.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, architecture and dataset-size studies, and additional visualizations. The paper also acknowledges the failure to preserve scarcely represented behaviors.
weaknesses: The central expressivity claim is not established by the evaluation. Performance recovery compares the best sampled latent return with the original dataset's return range on a few rewards; it does not measure reconstruction of individual policies, coverage of behavioral distributions, or preservation of the policy space. A representation containing only a few successful behaviors could score highly. Recovery above one can indicate improvement over a weak random-policy dataset without demonstrating broad generalization. Held-out behavioral reconstruction and coverage measurements are needed.

The connection between the formal occupancy-distribution objective and the implemented action-MSE loss is insufficiently justified. Small action discrepancies on uniformly sampled states do not generally bound trajectory or occupancy discrepancies without additional assumptions on dynamics and state coverage. Some uniformly sampled states are physically invalid, notably independently sampled sine and cosine coordinates in Reacher. Furthermore, maximizing an upper bound on behavioral divergence does not guarantee behavioral diversity, and reconstruction loss alone does not ensure that functionally equivalent policies receive similar latent codes.

The intrinsic-dimension conclusion substantially exceeds the evidence. Network-size variation is investigated primarily in Mountain Car, and recovering extrema of a few reward functions does not estimate intrinsic behavioral dimension. The fixed autoencoder has 10-unit internal layers, so the nominal 16D configurations are themselves constrained by narrower bottlenecks. The reported 121801:1 ratio describes latent-code dimensionality relative to policy weights, rather than demonstrated preservation of the full policy class or total model-storage compression.

Essential comparisons and ablations are missing. There is no matched comparison against a parameter-reconstruction autoencoder, random low-dimensional parameter subspaces, or relevant unsupervised skill and policy-manifold methods. Nor is there an ablation of novelty filtering. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate whether improvements arise from the proposed behavioral objective, generic dimensionality reduction, or dataset selection. The claimed novelty over the closely related approaches discussed in Appendix A remains primarily conceptual.

Evidence for practical adaptation advantages is narrow. Fine-tuning is evaluated only on Mountain Car and modified Reacher tasks; Hopper and HalfCheetah receive recovery measurements without downstream learning comparisons or absolute returns. Figure 4 also shows substantial asymptotic shortcomings on speed and height. Comparisons against training from scratch do not establish competitiveness with representation-pretraining methods, and no component-level compute or amortization analysis accompanies the sample-efficiency claims.

Several experimental details require clarification for reproducibility: the random-weight sampling range is unspecified; the main text and appendix disagree about Mountain Car termination for speed and height; and Appendix B describes 75 Mountain Car runs whereas Figure 4 reports 10. Extending completed learning curves under an assumed convergence condition also needs clearer justification. These ambiguities complicate interpretation of the reported comparisons.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: learning reusable, reward-free policy representations that make downstream optimization more efficient.

Reconstructing policy actions rather than exact network weights is a sensible approach to avoiding unnecessary parameter reconstruction. The resulting pipeline is straightforward and compatible with latent-space PGPE.

Experiments explore several latent dimensions, dataset sizes, and policy architectures, with multiple seeds and substantial implementation details. Figures 4–5 provide evidence of faster early learning on several Mountain Car and modified Reacher tasks, and the paper acknowledges failure on the height task.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving behavioral expressivity is not established by the evaluation. The performance-recovery metric measures the best sampled return relative to the dataset’s return range on a few rewards; it does not measure reconstruction of individual policies, occupancy distributions, or coverage of the behavior space. Recovering a few task maxima can coexist with losing most behaviors. Consequently, the claimed 121801:1 compression and conclusions about intrinsic dimensionality substantially exceed the evidence.

The connection between the formal objective and implemented loss is inadequately justified. Section 4 invokes a policy-divergence bound but substitutes empirical action-space L2 distance without establishing applicable assumptions or constants. Small action error on uniformly sampled states need not imply small occupancy-distribution error under the environment dynamics. Maximizing this proxy likewise does not ensure behavioral diversity. Reacher state sampling also independently samples sine and cosine coordinates, potentially emphasizing physically invalid states.

Essential comparisons and ablations are missing. There is no controlled comparison against parameter-reconstruction autoencoders, random low-dimensional parameter subspaces, or relevant policy-manifold and unsupervised skill-learning methods. Neither novelty filtering nor the behavioral loss is ablated. This makes it difficult to attribute improvements to the proposed contribution or establish its advantage over the closely related approaches discussed in Appendix A.

Evidence for downstream effectiveness is limited to Mountain Car and modified Reacher. Hopper and HalfCheetah provide only recovery ratios, without absolute returns or fine-tuning comparisons against competent task-trained policies. Exceeding the best return in a randomly generated policy dataset does not establish strong task performance. Moreover, Figure 4 shows substantial final-performance deficits on speed and height, and Figure 5 does not show consistent final-return superiority.

The intrinsic-dimension hypothesis is not directly tested. Network-size variation is studied only in Mountain Car, and no intrinsic-dimension estimator or reconstruction-versus-dimension analysis is provided. Randomly generated policy datasets may themselves occupy a restricted functional family. In addition, the fixed autoencoder contains 10-unit hidden layers, so the nominal 16-dimensional latent configuration is constrained by a narrower internal bottleneck.

Several experimental details weaken reproducibility and interpretation: the random policy-weight sampling range is unspecified; Appendix B reports 75 Mountain Car runs while Figure 4 reports 10; and the height/speed termination descriptions differ between Section 5 and Appendix B. Learning curves are extended beyond completed runs under an assumed convergence condition, which should be distinguished from observed training. The reported compression ratio also excludes the shared decoder, and the efficiency comparison lacks a breakdown of pretraining cost and its amortization across tasks.

strengths: The behavioral reconstruction objective is a sensible way to avoid penalizing functionally equivalent policy parameterizations. Combining it with reward-free policy collection and latent-space optimization provides a coherent, potentially useful framework.

The experiments demonstrate that very low-dimensional latent spaces can contain useful policies, with strong performance recovery for several Mountain Car configurations and improvements over the sampled policy datasets on several Hopper and HalfCheetah tasks.

Latent PGPE shows promising early learning performance on several Mountain Car and Reacher tasks. The paper also acknowledges a meaningful failure case: insufficient representation of high-performing height policies.
The appendix provides substantial architectural, optimization, and seed details, and several experiments report uncertainty across multiple runs.
weaknesses: The principal compression metric does not establish preservation of behavioral expressivity. Performance recovery compares the best sampled latent policy against the dataset's reward range for a few selected rewards; it does not measure reconstruction of individual policies, occupancy distributions, or coverage of diverse behaviors. Exceeding a randomly generated dataset's maximum return is encouraging, but does not demonstrate compression of the full policy space or retention of most of its expressivity.

The connection between the formal objective and the implemented loss is insufficiently justified. Section 4 replaces occupancy-distribution divergence with action-space MSE on sampled states without assumptions or a bound showing that this controls behavioral divergence. Small action errors can compound through dynamics. Moreover, uniformly sampled coordinate boxes can contain physically inconsistent states, particularly for Reacher's sine/cosine features. Behavioral reconstruction alone also does not ensure that equivalent policies receive nearby latent codes.

The intrinsic-dimension claim is substantially stronger than the evidence. Network-size variation is studied only in Mountain Car, without direct dimension estimates or controlled behavioral-complexity experiments. Appendix B additionally fixes a 10-unit hidden layer on both sides of the latent representation, so the nominal 16-dimensional configuration still passes through a bottleneck of at most 10 dimensions. This complicates interpreting the dimensionality sweep.

Critical comparisons and ablations are missing. There is no matched parameter-reconstruction autoencoder, random low-dimensional subspace, untrained decoder, or removal of novelty filtering. Closely related policy-manifold and generative-policy methods are discussed but not evaluated. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate the contribution of the proposed loss or establish the pipeline's advantage over simpler alternatives.

Downstream optimization is evaluated only on Mountain Car and modified Reacher tasks; Hopper and HalfCheetah receive compression evaluations but no fine-tuning comparisons. Figure 4 also shows substantial limitations on height and a lower final speed return than DDPG. The broad claims of superior performance and sample efficiency need more qualified wording, stronger reward-free pretraining baselines, and separate reporting of preprocessing/training costs and downstream interaction savings.

Several experimental details require clarification for reproducibility: the uniform policy-weight sampling range is unspecified, the Mountain Car fine-tuning description reports 75 runs while Figure 4 reports 10, and the main text and appendix disagree about termination for height and speed. The stated clockwise reward condition also appears inconsistent with its intended direction. These ambiguities affect the interpretation of the reported results.
